We spent about two years selling to everybody and calling it a strategy. The exercise that changed it took an afternoon. Somebody put our twenty best accounts on a wall and asked what they had in common, and the first three answers were useless. Big. Multinational. Complex. Then somebody said, their finance teams all have an internal auditor, and the room went quiet, because that was true of nineteen of the twenty and it was true of almost nobody we had been calling. From that afternoon we stopped describing our clients by size and started describing them by who was sitting in their finance team. Our pipeline got smaller and the close rate roughly doubled. And the uncomfortable part is that the information had been in the building the whole time. Nobody had ever written the sentence.

The person who signs is not the person you are selling to, and I wish somebody had told me that ten years earlier. The person who signs wants the risk explained in two lines. The person who actually decides is usually one level down, and she is the one who has lived with the old system, and she has a story about the week it failed. That person is your champion, whether you have identified her or not, and she is arguing your case in rooms you will never be in. So the question I ask now, in every first meeting, is: who else is going to be affected by this, and what happened to them last year? It sounds like small talk and it is the most commercial question in the conversation.
